title: Runtime plugin safety and deployment checklist
author: Asha Verma
body:
Overview
-------

Purpose: This page documents a prescriptive checklist, gating criteria, and automated tests required to safely introduce runtime plugins (kernel adapters, scheduler plugins, or sidecar instrumentations) into Redwood's inference runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, kernel authors, and release owners.

Scope: applies to any code that executes inside the serving runtime process or modifies kernel scheduling behavior, including:
- third-party kernel drivers or accelerator adapters
- custom scheduler plugins and admission controllers
- observability sidecars that inject telemetry or sampling hooks
- experimental serialization/deserialization modules that touch request/response flows

Goals
-----
- Minimize production blast radius for plugin rollouts.
- Ensure deterministic performance and memory behaviour under peaky traffic.
- Guarantee observability and fast rollback on regressions.
- Provide reproducible benchmarking and profiling steps for acceptance gates.

Key risks and failure modes
-------------------------
- Non-deterministic kernel latency growth (tail latency spikes).
- Memory fragmentation or soft-ooms from plugin state leaks.
- Priority inversion introduced by scheduler hooks.
- Telemetry amplification causing control-plane overload.
- Silent semantic changes to model inputs/outputs (format drift).

Pre-deployment checklist (must pass all gates)
--------------------------------------------
1) Code & static safety
   - PR has clear README describing purpose, public interfaces, and intended failure modes.
   - Static analysis run: no unsafe deserialization, no unbounded allocations without guardrails.
   - Third-party dependencies reviewed for license and CVEs (security team sign-off for >= moderate).

2) Unit and integration tests
   - Unit coverage >= 80% for new code paths.
   - Integration tests exercise: request lifecycle (begin, KV cache lookup, kernel dispatch, response), error injection (timeouts, kernel failure), and graceful degradation.
   - Fuzz harness enabled for parser/serializer plugins.

3) Performance and resource budgets
   - Microbenchmarks added to the repo with the submitter-provided baseline and expected overhead.
   - Memory budget defined: max RSS delta <= 5% on steady-state synthetic workload; peak transient <= 15% with GC/eviction verified.
   - Max per-request added latency budget: p50 <= 1ms, p95 <= 5ms (defaults; product/route owners may tighten).

4) Profiling & observability hooks
   - Traces: plugin exposes span(s) with standardized tags: plugin.name, plugin.version, request.id, kernel.variant.
   - Metrics: must emit per-plugin counters for invocations, errors, and duration histogram (Prometheus format).
   - Logs: structured JSON logs with level, timestamp, request.id, and short context.

5) Canary and rollout plan
   - Canary matrix prepared (traffic slices, model variants, sequence lengths).
   - Rollout strategy defined: staged percentages 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30m observation windows.
   - Automatic rollback rules enumerated (see SLO gates below).

6) Security and data handling
   - No write access to persistent customer data outside defined KV caches unless explicitly approved.
   - KMS/HSM integration validated if plugin requests keys.

Acceptance gating: telemetry & SLOs
--------------------------------
The plugin rollout must satisfy these gating rules during every canary window:
- Error rate: plugin-specific error_rate <= baseline_error_rate + 0.2% absolute AND service-level errors not increased.
- Latency regressions: p95 latency of route using plugin must not exceed baseline p95 + 10% or +50ms (whichever smaller).
- Resource signals: node memory pressure and GPU memory delta stable (no increase in OS OOM kills).
- Kernel health: no increase in kernel queue length > 2x baseline sustained > 5 minutes.
- Observability completeness: 99% of requests must include plugin spans and metric emission.

If any gate fails, the automated rollout must immediately revert to the previous release and file an incident.

Canary and rollout step-by-step procedure
---------------------------------------
1) Pre-canary (run in staging):
   - Deploy plugin build to staging runtime cluster.
   - Run synthetic benchmark plan: 30m steady-state, 5m microburst at 10x, and 10k unique prompt corpus replay.
   - Validate telemetry completeness and that integration tests pass on the canary lab.

2) Canary 1% (production shadow+1%):
   - Route 1% of production traffic through the plugin-managed path; mirror requests to comparison path.
   - Monitor gates for 30 minutes.
   - If green, promote to 5%. If not, rollback and open triage.

3) Canary 5% and 25%:
   - At each stage, run targeted microbenchmarks for the active model variants and sequence length distributions.
   - Run the profiling playbook (see Profiling section).

4) Full rollout:
   - Once at 100% for 60 minutes with no gate violations, mark feature as GA.

Profiling and benchmarking playbook (quick reference)
---------------------------------------------------
- Tools: perfbench (internal), microtrace (span collector), nvprof/nvtx (for accelerator plugins), pprof (CPU), jemalloc statistics.
- Synthetic load: use the inference-workload-replay tool with the golden corpus of route-specific prompts. Example command:
  ./inference-workload-replay --route my-route --duration 30m --qps 250 --seq-distribution seq-dist.json --compare baseline-build:12345

- Kernel-level profiling: run a 10-minute mixed workload and collect nvtx ranges labelled plugin:entry and plugin:exit. Example nvprof invocation:
  NVPROF_LOGFILE=nvlog.json nvprof --profile-child-processes --export-profile nvprofile.nvprof -- ./runtime --plugin path/to/plugin.so

- Memory and allocator checks:
  - Capture jemalloc stats pre/post using: curl localhost:9100/allocator/stats | jq '.'
  - Ensure active fragment count delta < 3% for steady-state runs.

- Tracing validation: verify every request has plugin span and that duration histogram aligns with microbenchmarks. Use microtrace query:
  microtrace query "service=runtime AND plugin.name=MY_PLUGIN" --stats p50,p95,p99

Test matrix (text table)
----------------------
Route | Model variant | Seq lengths | QPS profile | Required checks
------|---------------|------------|------------|----------------
search-low | base-merged | [8,32] | 200 | latency p95, mem delta, spans
chat-long | llama-xl | [64,512] | 50 | p95, kvcache correctness, distributional checks
batch-embed | embedder-v2 | [1,1] | 800 | throughput, batching overhead, histogram stability

Rollback and incident triage playbook
-----------------------------------
1) If automatic rollback triggered:
   - Oncall patches route to prior build and escalates to runtime-oncall and plugin owner.
   - Collect artifacts: traces (microtrace TTL 7d), nvprof logs, jemalloc dumps, kernel queue length logs, and pod-level logs.

2) Triage checklist (first 30 minutes):
   - Reproduce failure in canary lab with identical traffic profile.
   - Check for memory leaks: run 15-minute soak with heap snapshot.
   - Confirm whether failure is semantic (input/output differences) or performance (latency/memory).

3) Post-incident:
   - Fill incident template with root cause hypothesis, mitigation, test to prevent regressions, and owner for follow-up.
   - Schedule a 2-hour postmortem within 72 hours if customer impact occurred.

Operational runbook extracts (for oncall)
---------------------------------------
- Quick checks when alerted:
  1) Query: Prometheus - plugin:errors_total{plugin=\"MY_PLUGIN\"} by (instance) over 10m.
     Alert threshold: > 1% of total requests.
  2) Kernel queue depth: runtime_kernel_queue_length{instance} > 2x baseline for 5m.
  3) Memory: node_memory_available_bytes and container_memory_rss_bytes trend.
  4) Trace sampling: microtrace sample rate and presence of plugin spans; if missing, fail closed (treat as regression).

Ownership, signoff and documentation requirements
------------------------------------------------
- Code owner: must be an engineering team with 24/7 oncall coverage.
- Release owner: a named engineer responsible for canary monitoring and rollback.
- Documentation: README, deployment manifest, schema for metrics and spans, and example benchmark artifacts must be committed to the plugin repo.

Appendix A: sample deployment fragment (Kubernetes)
-------------------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: runtime-plugin-myplugin
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        runtime.redwood.com/plugin-name: "myplugin"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: runtime
        image: ghcr.io/redwood/runtime:canary-2028-01-10
        args: ["--plugin", "/opt/plugins/myplugin.so", "--plugin-metrics-prefix", "plugin_myplugin_"]
      - name: plugin-sidecar
        image: ghcr.io/redwood/plugin-sidecar:1.0.0
        env:
        - name: PLUGIN_MODE
          value: "sandboxed"

Appendix B: sample validation script (bash snippet)
-------------------------------------------------
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# run quick smoke and collect traces
./inference-workload-replay --route search-low --duration 5m --qps 100 || { echo 'replay failed'; exit 1; }
microtrace query "service=runtime AND plugin.name=myplugin" --stats p95 || { echo 'tracing missing'; exit 1; }

Appendix C: FAQ
---------------
Q: What qualifies as a plugin vs an integration?
A: Plugins execute inside the runtime or affect scheduling. Integrations that run externally (e.g. separate microservices) are treated as normal service integrations and follow a different checklist.

Q: How do I request higher latency budgets for experimental features?
A: Submit a feature request to the runtime-product channel with workload benchmarks and target routes. Product must approve any SLO changes before canary.
